bhrigu.name: Bhrigu
bhrigu.description: Bhrigu is the ancestor of the Bhargava priestly clan, whom the Rig Veda credits with bringing fire to humankind. The Brahmanas and Taittiriya Upanishad know him as Bhrigu Varuni, son and pupil of Varuna, while the Puranas count him among the mind-born sons of Brahma. His line includes Chyavana, Shukracharya, Jamadagni and Parashurama.
bhrigu.story: Once the sages gathered on the Sarasvati argued about which of the three great gods was supreme, and they sent Bhrigu to find out. At Brahma's court he pointedly failed to bow, and Brahma flushed with anger but held back for the sake of his son. On Kailasa, Shiva rose to embrace him, but Bhrigu rebuffed him as an impure wanderer of cremation grounds; Shiva raised his trident until Parvati calmed him. In Vaikuntha, Bhrigu found Vishnu resting with Lakshmi and kicked him in the chest. Vishnu rose at once, begged pardon for not greeting his guest, and pressed the sage's foot, asking whether it was hurt. He said he would wear the mark on his chest forever. Overwhelmed, Bhrigu went back and declared Vishnu the greatest of the gods.
bhrigu.abode: Bhrigu's hermitage (associated with Bhrigukaccha / Bharuch on the Narmada)
variations: Vedic texts make him the son of Varuna; the Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) has him born from the fire of Varuna's sacrifice; the Puranas make him a mind-born son of Brahma.

The test of the Trimurti (Bhagavata 10.89) ends in praise of Vishnu; the Padma Purana version has Bhrigu curse Shiva and Brahma, and the Matsya Purana tells of him cursing Vishnu to be born among mortals.
Astrological tradition attributes the Bhrigu Samhita to him.

atri.name: Atri
atri.description: Atri is the seer-family behind the fifth mandala of the Rig Veda and one of the Saptarishis in both the Vedic and Puranic lists. The Rig Veda remembers the Ashvins rescuing him from a burning pit and his restoring the eclipsed Sun. In the Puranas he and his wife Anasuya are the parents of Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa.
atri.story: Atri and Anasuya withdrew to Mount Riksha to beg the Lord of the universe for a son like himself. Atri stood on one leg, living on air, for a hundred years, until the heat of his tapas rose from his head as fire and scorched the three worlds. Then Brahma on his swan, Vishnu on Garuda and Shiva on his bull appeared before him together. Astonished, Atri asked why three had come when he had prayed to one. The gods smiled and said they were one reality, and since he had meditated on that one, each would be born as his son. So Soma was born from Brahma's portion, Dattatreya from Vishnu's, and the fiery Durvasa from Shiva's.
sources: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Rama at Atri's hermitage)
variations: The Vishnu Purana and Harivamsha say Soma was born from Atri's eyes; the Bhagavata makes Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa sons of Atri and Anasuya as portions of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
Later tradition identifies the Svarbhanu of Rig Veda 5.40 with Rahu, the eclipse demon.

anasuya.name: Anasuya
anasuya.description: Anasuya ('free from envy') is the wife of the sage Atri and a model of chastity and ascetic power. In the Ramayana she welcomes Sita at Chitrakuta and gives her gifts that never fade. The Puranas make her the mother of Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa.
anasuya.story: When Rama, Sita and Lakshmana reached Atri's hermitage, the sage introduced his aged wife, whose tapas was legendary. During a ten-year drought she had brought forth fruits and roots and made the Ganga flow through the forest as the Mandakini; at the gods' request she had even turned ten nights into one. Sita bowed to her, and Anasuya praised her for following her husband into exile, teaching her that a devoted wife is her husband's truest companion in dharma. Pleased by Sita's humility, she gave her a celestial garland, garments, ornaments and an unguent that would never fade or lose its fragrance. Then she asked Sita to tell how Rama had won her at the svayamvara, and listened with delight as night fell on the forest.
sources: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (sargas 117–119 in the vulgate)
variations: The Bhagavata makes her a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti; the Vishnu Purana a daughter of Daksha and Prasuti.
A popular later legend (in Dattatreya traditions) tells how Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva came to test her chastity and she turned them into infants, after which they were born as her sons.

kashyapa.name: Kashyapa
kashyapa.description: Kashyapa is a Vedic seer and, in the epics and Puranas, the great progenitor: son of Marichi and husband of thirteen daughters of Daksha. Through Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kadru and Vinata he fathered the Adityas, Daityas, Danavas, Nagas, Garuda and Aruna, so gods and demons alike are Kashyapas. He is one of the Saptarishis in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age.
kashyapa.story: One evening Diti, burning with desire for a son, came to Kashyapa just as he had finished his sacrificial offerings. He begged her to wait, for it was twilight, the hour when Shiva and his ghostly hosts roam and people must be pure and watchful. Diti would not be put off, and Kashyapa gave in. Afterwards, ashamed, she feared Shiva's anger, and Kashyapa told her sadly that because she had conceived at that forbidden hour she would bear two fearsome sons who would torment the worlds, until the Lord himself descended to destroy them. Yet, moved by her repentance, he promised that one grandson would be a great devotee of Vishnu. The twins were Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu, and the grandson was Prahlada.
kashyapa.abode: Hermitage in the Himalaya; Kashmir (Kashyapa-mira) is traditionally named after him
variations: The number and names of his wives vary; the Mahabharata and Puranas usually give thirteen daughters of Daksha.
In the Rig Veda the Maruts are sons of Rudra and Prishni, but in the Ramayana and Puranas they are born from Diti's embryo, which Indra split.

angiras.name: Angiras
angiras.description: Angiras is the ancestor of the Angirasa priestly clan, which the Rig Veda calls the ancient fathers who won back the hidden cows and the light. Agni himself is called the first Angiras, and the Atharva Veda was once known as the Atharvangirasa. Later tradition counts Angiras among Brahma's mind-born sons and the Saptarishis, and makes him the father of Brihaspati.
angiras.story: In the time of the fathers, the Panis hid the cows of the gods, and with them the dawn's light, deep inside the rock-cave of Vala. The divine bitch Sarama tracked them across the waters, but the Panis only mocked her. Then the Angirases, the ancient singers, came with Indra and Brihaspati to the mountain. They sang their sacred hymns, and the power of their chant, together with Indra's might, split the rock. Vala broke open, the bellowing cows came out into the light, and the dawn and the Sun shone on the world again. The Rig Veda returns to this deed again and again, for the Angirases' song showed that a true prayer can open what force alone cannot.
variations: In the Rig Veda the Angirases are mostly a group of ancestral priests; the epics and Puranas turn Angiras into a single Prajapati.
His wife is Shraddha (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata and Smriti (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana.

pulastya.name: Pulastya
pulastya.description: Pulastya is one of Brahma's mind-born sons and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. Through his son Vishrava he is the grandfather of Kubera, Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana, so the rakshasas of Lanka are called Paulastyas. He also appears as a teacher of Bhishma and as the sage who blessed Parashara to compose a Purana.
pulastya.story: Pulastya went to do tapas on the slopes of Meru, near the hermitage of the royal sage Trinabindu. The daughters of nearby sages and nymphs kept coming there to sing, dance and play, breaking his concentration. Annoyed, Pulastya declared that any maiden who came into his sight would become pregnant. The others stayed away, but Trinabindu's daughter had not heard the warning and wandered there looking for her friends. She saw the sage, found herself with child and ran home in dismay. Trinabindu understood what had happened and gave her to Pulastya as his wife. Pleased with her devoted service, the sage promised her a son as learned as himself, and she bore Vishrava, who became the father of Kubera and Ravana.
variations: The Mahabharata says the rakshasas, vanaras and yakshas were all Pulastya's offspring.
The Bhagavata names his wife Havirbhu (Kardama's daughter) and his sons Agastya and Vishrava; the Vishnu Purana names his wife Priti (Daksha's daughter).

pulaha.name: Pulaha
pulaha.description: Pulaha is one of the six (later seven or ten) mind-born sons of Brahma and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. The Mahabharata makes him the progenitor of wild creatures and the Kimpurushas. His hermitage on the Gandaki, Pulahashrama, is a holy place in the Puranas.
pulaha.story: When Brahma wanted to populate the world, sons sprang from his mind, and Pulaha was born from his navel, some say, or from his ear. Unlike his brothers, whose children were sages and gods, Pulaha became the father of the wild world. The Mahabharata says his offspring were the sharabhas, lions, tigers, bears and wolves, along with the Kimpurushas, the half-human beings of the mountains. Pulaha later withdrew to a hermitage on the banks of the Gandaki, where the river's stones carry the marks of Vishnu. The Bhagavata tells that King Bharata, giving up his throne, came to this Pulahashrama to spend his last years in worship, and it has remained a place of pilgrimage ever since.
variations: The Bhagavata (3.12) says Pulaha was born from Brahma's navel; other Puranas give different parts of Brahma's body.
The Vishnu Purana makes Kardama a son of Pulaha and Kshama; the Bhagavata makes Kardama born from Brahma's shadow and has Pulaha marry Kardama's daughter Gati.

kratu.name: Kratu
kratu.description: Kratu is one of Brahma's mind-born sons and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. His name means 'willpower' or 'sacrificial intent'. He is best known as the father of the Valakhilyas, sixty thousand thumb-sized ascetics who attend the Sun's chariot.
kratu.story: Kratu's sons, the Valakhilyas, were each no bigger than a thumb, yet their tapas was immense. When Kashyapa held a sacrifice to gain a son, Indra carried a mountain of firewood while the Valakhilyas struggled together under a single leaf-stalk. Indra laughed and stepped over them. Stung, the tiny sages began a new sacrifice to bring forth a second Indra who would be a terror to the first. The frightened king of the gods ran to Kashyapa, who persuaded the ascetics not to overturn Brahma's order. The power of their rite would instead go into a son who would be 'Indra' of the birds. So the Valakhilyas' tapas went into the birth of Garuda, and they themselves withdrew to follow the chariot of the Sun.
variations: His wife is Sannati (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana and Kriya (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata.
The Mahabharata tells the Valakhilya episode without naming Kratu as their father; the Puranas supply the link.

marichi.name: Marichi
marichi.description: Marichi ('ray of light') is usually named first among Brahma's mind-born sons and heads the Puranic list of Saptarishis for the first age. He is the father of Kashyapa and so the forefather of gods, asuras and the Solar dynasty. The Bhagavad Gita names a Marichi as chief of the Maruts.
marichi.story: At the wedding of Rama and Sita in Mithila, the family priest Vashistha stood up to recite the lineage of the Ikshvakus, as custom required. He began at the very beginning: the eternal Brahma, born of the unmanifest, had a son Marichi. Marichi's son was Kashyapa, and Kashyapa's son was Vivasvan, the Sun. From Vivasvan came Manu, the first king, and from Manu came Ikshvaku, founder of Ayodhya's royal line. Generation by generation Vashistha named the kings down to Dasharatha and his sons. The genealogy shows why Marichi is so honoured, for this ray of Brahma's mind stands at the head of the solar kings and, through Kashyapa, of the Adityas and Daityas alike.
sources: Ramayana, Bala Kanda 1.70 and Ayodhya Kanda 2.110 (Ikshvaku genealogy)
variations: His wife is Kala (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata and Sambhuti (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana.
Commentators often treat the Marichi of Gita 10.21, chief of the Maruts, as distinct from the Prajapati.
In Jain tradition a Marichi, grandson of Rishabhanatha, is an earlier birth of Mahavira; this figure is unrelated to the Puranic Prajapati.

vashistha.name: Vashistha
vashistha.description: Vashistha is the seer-family of the seventh mandala of the Rig Veda, where he is priest to King Sudas and is said to be born of Mitra and Varuna. In the epics he is the royal priest of the Ikshvakus, guru of Rama, owner of the wish-granting cow and the great rival of Vishvamitra. He is a Saptarishi in every list, and his wife Arundhati is the model of marital devotion.
vashistha.story: King Vishvamitra, returning from a campaign, stopped at Vashistha's hermitage, and the sage fed his whole army with delicacies produced by his cow Shabala. Amazed, the king demanded the cow, offering thousands of cattle and even his kingdom. Vashistha refused, and Vishvamitra had her dragged away. Weeping, Shabala broke free and ran back to her master, and at his word she poured out armies of warriors who destroyed the king's forces. Vishvamitra's sons attacked Vashistha, and he burned them to ashes with a single cry. The king then won divine weapons from Shiva and loosed them all, even the Brahmastra, but Vashistha stood firm with only his staff, which swallowed every weapon. Vishvamitra cried out that a kshatriya's strength is worthless beside a brahmin's power, and set out to become a brahmarshi himself.
vashistha.abode: Hermitage in the Himalaya; royal court of Ayodhya; the star Mizar in Ursa Major
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Vashistha–Vishvamitra and Vasus episodes)
variations: In the Rig Veda he is born of Mitra and Varuna at the sight of Urvashi; the Puranas make him Brahma's mind-born son, and explain the two births by saying Nimi's curse forced him to be reborn from Mitra and Varuna.
The cow is Shabala in the Ramayana and Nandini (Kamadhenu's daughter) in the Mahabharata.
The rivalry with Vishvamitra may reflect the two sages' competition for King Sudas's patronage in the Rig Veda; later texts turn it into a contest between brahmin and kshatriya power.
The Yoga Vasishtha, a late philosophical work, is framed as his teaching to Rama.

arundhati.name: Arundhati
arundhati.description: Arundhati is the wife of Vashistha and the ideal of marital fidelity. In Vedic domestic ritual the bride is shown the star Arundhati (Alcor) beside Vashistha (Mizar) in the Great Bear as a sign of constancy. The Mahabharata praises her tapas and says she alone among the sages' wives could not be impersonated.
arundhati.story: Agni once fell in love with the wives of the Seven Sages as he blazed in their sacrificial fires, and he wasted away with longing. Svaha, daughter of Daksha, loved Agni and wanted to win him, so she took the form of each wife in turn and went to him, flying off afterwards as a bird. She took the shapes of six of the wives, but she could not take the form of Arundhati, whose devotion to Vashistha and whose tapas were beyond imitation. Rumour soon spread that the sages' wives had been with Agni, and six of the rishis gave up their wives, who became the Krittikas, the Pleiades. Only Arundhati stayed at her husband's side, and so she shines beside him in the northern sky.
arundhati.abode: Vashistha's hermitage; the star Alcor beside Mizar
sources: Grihya Sutras (marriage rite: showing the bride Dhruva and Arundhati)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva (birth of Skanda, Svaha episode)
variations: The Bhagavata makes her a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti; the Vishnu Purana names Vashistha's wife Urja, daughter of Daksha.
The Shiva Purana says she was once Sandhya, a mind-born daughter of Brahma, who was reborn as Arundhati, daughter of the sage Medhatithi.
The Atharva Veda uses arundhati as the name of a healing plant; her identity as Vashistha's wife comes from later ritual and epic texts.

vishvamitra.name: Vishvamitra
vishvamitra.description: Vishvamitra is the seer-family of the third mandala of the Rig Veda, which contains the Gayatri mantra (3.62.10). The epics tell how this king of the Kushika line gave up his throne after being humbled by Vashistha and, through enormous tapas, became a brahmarshi. He is Rama's teacher in the Ramayana and a Saptarishi in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age.
vishvamitra.story: King Trishanku wanted to go to heaven in his own body. Vashistha refused to perform the rite, and Vashistha's sons cursed the king to become an outcaste. Vishvamitra, still at odds with Vashistha, took pity on him and began the sacrifice himself. By the strength of his tapas Trishanku rose into the sky, but Indra pushed him back, and the king came tumbling down crying for help. Vishvamitra shouted 'Stop!', and Trishanku hung in mid-air. In fury the sage began to create a second universe, with new constellations in the southern sky and even a new set of gods. The frightened gods came to terms. Trishanku would stay, head downward, shining among the new stars Vishvamitra had made, and those stars would last as long as the worlds endure.
weapons: divine astras (won from Shiva and passed to Rama)
vishvamitra.abode: Siddhashrama; hermitage on the Kaushiki river
variations: The Ramayana tells his rise to brahmarshi in stages (rajarshi, rishi, maharshi, brahmarshi); the Mahabharata and Puranas differ in detail.
In the Aitareya Brahmana he adopts Shunahshepa as his eldest son Devarata; in the Ramayana he teaches Shunahshepa the hymns that save him.
The Harishchandra ordeal is told in the Markandeya and Devi Bhagavata Puranas; the Aitareya Brahmana's Harishchandra story does not include Vishvamitra's persecution.

jamadagni.name: Jamadagni
jamadagni.description: Jamadagni is a Rig Vedic seer of the Bhrigu clan and one of the Saptarishis in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age. In the epics he is the son of Richika, husband of Renuka and father of Parashurama. His murder by the sons of Kartavirya Arjuna led Parashurama to wage war on the kshatriyas.
jamadagni.story: Renuka went to the river to fetch water and saw King Chitraratha sporting with his wives. For a moment she was stirred with longing. When she returned, Jamadagni saw by his ascetic insight what had passed in her mind and, in anger, ordered his sons one by one to kill her. The four eldest froze in horror, and he cursed them to lose their reason. Then the youngest, Rama (Parashurama), came in and at his father's word struck off his mother's head with his axe. The sage's anger cooled, and he offered his obedient son any boon. Parashurama asked that his mother live again with no memory of what had happened, that his brothers be restored, and that he himself be unconquered in battle and long-lived. All was granted.
jamadagni.abode: Hermitage on the Narmada; traditionally linked with Jamadagni-ashrama sites
sources: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Surya's umbrella and sandals)
variations: The Mahabharata says Kartavirya carried off the calf of Jamadagni's sacrificial cow; later Puranas and folk tellings call the cow Kamadhenu or Sushila.
In the Bhagavata, Kartavirya's sons behead Jamadagni to avenge their father; in some versions Renuka is also wounded.
His mother Satyavati was Vishvamitra's sister, and the Mahabharata's story of the swapped sacrificial porridge links the two sages' natures.

gautama.name: Gautama Maharishi
gautama.description: Gotama Rahugana is the seer of Rig Veda hymns 1.74–93, and a Gotama is one of the seven sages in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's list. In the epics Gautama is the husband of Ahalya, who curses her and Indra, and the Puranas credit him with bringing the Godavari to earth. Tradition generally treats these as one sage, though the identification is not certain.
gautama.story: During a long drought, Gautama's tapas kept his hermitage at Brahmagiri green, and he fed the sages who came to him for shelter. When the rains returned, some of them wanted to leave, and they set loose an illusory cow in his rice-field. The Brahma Purana says Ganesha, acting for Parvati, sent it to draw Ganga away from Shiva. When Gautama drove it away with a blade of grass, the cow fell dead, and he was blamed for killing a cow. To cleanse the sin, Gautama worshipped Shiva with great devotion until Shiva released a stream of the Ganga from his matted hair onto Brahmagiri. There it became the Godavari, also called Gautami, which flows past Tryambakeshwar to the eastern sea.
variations: Whether the Rig Vedic Gotama Rahugana, Ahalya's husband and the Gautama of the Godavari legend are one sage is uncertain; tradition tends to merge them.
Akshapada Gautama, author of the Nyaya Sutras, and the Gautama of the Dharmasutra are usually treated as different figures.

ahalya.name: Ahalya
ahalya.description: Ahalya is the wife of the sage Gautama, whom Indra seduced in her husband's form. Gautama's curse and her release by Rama is one of the best-known episodes of the Ramayana. She is counted among the Panchakanya, five women whose names are recited at dawn to remove sin.
ahalya.story: One morning, while Gautama was away, Indra came to the hermitage disguised as the sage and asked Ahalya to lie with him. In Valmiki's telling she knew who he was and agreed out of curiosity about the king of the gods. As Indra slipped away, the real Gautama came back from his bath. Seeing everything, he cursed Indra to lose his manhood and cursed Ahalya to live invisible in the hermitage for thousands of years, living on air and lying in ashes, until Rama came. Long afterwards Vishvamitra brought Rama and Lakshmana to the silent hermitage. As Rama entered, Ahalya appeared again, radiant. The princes touched her feet, she welcomed them as guests, flowers rained from the sky, and Gautama returned to take her back.
variations: The Brahmanas only mention Indra as Ahalya's lover in a ritual formula, without condemning either of them.
In Valmiki's Bala Kanda she knowingly consents; in the Uttara Kanda, many Puranas and later retellings she is deceived and innocent.
Valmiki's curse makes her invisible and ascetic; from the Raghuvamsha, Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas onward she is turned to stone and freed by the touch of Rama's foot.
The Uttara Kanda says Brahma created her and gave her to Gautama; the Mahabharata and Harivamsha make her the daughter of the Puru king Mudgala.

bharadvaja.name: Bharadvaja
bharadvaja.description: Bharadvaja is the seer-family of the sixth mandala of the Rig Veda, son of Brihaspati and a Saptarishi in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age. In the Ramayana he hosts Rama and later Bharata at his hermitage at Prayaga. In the Mahabharata he is the father of Drona, and Ayurvedic tradition says he received medicine from Indra.
bharadvaja.story: Bharadvaja was so devoted to the Vedas that he spent three whole lifetimes studying them in celibacy. As he lay old and weak at the end of the third, Indra came and asked what he would do with a fourth life. 'I would spend it studying the Veda,' said Bharadvaja. Indra then showed him three huge mountains that had never been seen before, took a handful from each, and said: 'These mountains are the three Vedas, and these three handfuls are all you have learned. The Veda is endless.' Indra then taught him the Savitra fire rite, by which he could know the infinite Veda through the fire. Bharadvaja performed it and reached the world of heaven.
bharadvaja.abode: Hermitage at Prayaga, at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna
variations: The Puranas say he was born to Brihaspati and Mamata, his brother Utathya's wife, abandoned, and given by the Maruts to King Bharata, who adopted him.
A disciple named Bharadvaja goes with Valmiki in the opening of the Ramayana; whether he is the same as the Vedic seer is unclear.

dadhichi.name: Dadhichi (Dadhyanch)
dadhichi.description: Dadhyanch Atharvana appears in the Rig Veda as the seer who taught the Ashvins the secret Madhu-vidya through a horse's head, and with whose bones Indra struck down his enemies. In the epics and Puranas, as Dadhichi, he gives up his life so that his bones can be made into the vajra that kills Vritra. Shaiva Puranas also praise him as a devotee of Shiva who opposed Daksha.
dadhichi.story: The demon Vritra had swallowed the waters and driven the gods from heaven, and no weapon could harm him. Vishnu told the gods that only a weapon made from the bones of the sage Dadhichi could defeat him. Ashamed but desperate, Indra and the gods went to his hermitage and asked him for his body. Dadhichi smiled and said the body is only lent to us and is best given for the good of the worlds. Seated in yoga, he withdrew his life-breath and left his body. The divine craftsman Vishvakarma then shaped his bones into the vajra, the thunderbolt. Armed with it, Indra fought Vritra, killed him and set free the waters, and Dadhichi's gift has been a byword for sacrifice ever since.
dadhichi.abode: Hermitage on the Sarasvati; Naimisharanya (in later tradition)
variations: In the Rig Veda, Indra slays foes with the bones of Dadhyanch; the full self-sacrifice story comes from the Mahabharata and Puranas.
The Rig Veda calls Dadhyanch a son of Atharvan; some Puranas make Dadhichi a son of Chyavana and Sukanya.
The Linga Purana says he defeated Vishnu in a dispute over King Kshuva; Vaishnava texts do not share this episode.

chyavana.name: Chyavana
chyavana.description: Chyavana is the aged sage whom the Rig Veda praises the Ashvins for making young again. The Brahmanas and the Mahabharata tell how he married Princess Sukanya and won the Ashvins a share of the soma sacrifice. He is a son of Bhrigu and an ancestor of Jamadagni and Parashurama.
chyavana.story: Having been restored to youth by the Ashvins, Chyavana kept his promise to them. At King Sharyati's sacrifice he rose to offer the divine physicians a cup of soma, which the gods had always refused them. Indra objected that the Ashvins were only healers who mixed with mortals, not worthy of soma. Chyavana ignored him, and as he lifted the cup Indra raised the thunderbolt to strike. With one glance Chyavana froze Indra's arm. From the sacrificial fire he then called forth Mada, 'Intoxication', a monster so huge its jaws spanned earth and sky, which rushed at Indra to swallow him. Terrified, Indra gave in and granted the Ashvins their share. Chyavana then divided Mada into drink, women, dice and hunting.
chyavana.abode: Hermitage by a lake near the Narmada (Sharyati's land)
variations: In the Shatapatha Brahmana the Ashvins win their soma share by learning from Sukanya that they are 'incomplete'; the Mahabharata adds Indra's opposition and the demon Mada.
The Mahabharata names Chyavana's son Aurva by Arushi; some Puranas give his sons by Sukanya as Apnavana and Dadhicha.

sukanya.name: Sukanya
sukanya.description: Sukanya is the daughter of King Sharyati, son of Manu, and the wife of the aged sage Chyavana. Her loyalty, even when tempted by the Ashvins, led to her husband being made young again. Her story is first told in the Shatapatha Brahmana and retold in the Mahabharata and Puranas.
sukanya.story: Sukanya was playing in the forest when she saw two lights shining from an anthill and poked them with a thorn. They were the eyes of the ancient sage Chyavana, buried in his tapas. Her father's army was struck with sickness until King Sharyati made amends by giving Sukanya to the blinded old man. One day the Ashvins, the handsome twin physicians, found her bathing and urged her to leave her withered husband for one of them. She refused and told them they were themselves 'incomplete'. Curious, they promised to make Chyavana young if she would explain. She agreed, and the three went into a pool. Three identical youths came out, and Sukanya picked out her husband. Then she told the Ashvins they had been left out of the gods' sacrifice at Kurukshetra.
variations: In the Shatapatha Brahmana she wins the rejuvenation by telling the Ashvins why they are incomplete; in the Mahabharata and Bhagavata she must identify her husband among three identical youths.
In the Devi Bhagavata she recognises Chyavana through the grace of the Goddess.

agastya.name: Agastya
agastya.description: Agastya is the seer of Rig Veda hymns 1.165–191, born with Vashistha from the seed of Mitra and Varuna in a jar. The epics tell how he humbled the Vindhya mountains, drank the ocean, digested the demon Vatapi and armed Rama with divine weapons. In Tamil tradition he is Agathiyar, father of Tamil grammar and the Siddha tradition.
agastya.story: In the forest the asura brothers Ilvala and Vatapi killed brahmins by a cruel trick. Vatapi would turn himself into a goat, Ilvala would cook him and serve him to a guest, and then Ilvala would call his brother's name. Vatapi would burst out of the guest's belly, killing him. Agastya, needing wealth for his wife Lopamudra, came to Ilvala, who served him the usual meal. Agastya ate every bite, and when Ilvala called out, 'Vatapi, come out!', the sage just smiled, patted his stomach and said, 'He has been digested.' Only a belch came out. In the Ramayana, Ilvala then rushed at him in fury, and Agastya burned him to ashes with a blazing look, freeing the southern forests from their terror.
agastya.abode: Hermitage south of the Vindhyas (Panchavati region); Pothigai hills (Tamil tradition); the star Canopus
sources: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Anushasana Parva (Nahusha)
variations: In the Mahabharata Ilvala is subdued and gives Agastya wealth; in the Ramayana Agastya burns him to death.
The Aditya Hridaya, which Agastya teaches Rama before the final battle, is in the vulgate Yuddha Kanda but not in the Critical Edition.
The Bhagavata makes him a son of Pulastya and Havirbhu, unlike the Vedic birth from Mitra and Varuna.
Tamil tradition, and the Skanda Purana, say Shiva sent him south to balance the earth during Shiva's wedding, and that Murugan taught him Tamil.

lopamudra.name: Lopamudra
lopamudra.description: Lopamudra is the wife of Agastya and the woman who speaks in Rig Veda 1.179, where she urges her ascetic husband to turn to married love. The Mahabharata says Agastya created her from the finest features of all creatures and gave her to the king of Vidarbha to raise. Shri Vidya tradition honours her as a great devotee of the goddess Lalita Tripura Sundari.
lopamudra.story: Agastya once saw his ancestors hanging head-down in a pit. They told him they would fall unless he had a son to carry on their line. Finding no woman worthy of him, the sage made a girl from the most beautiful parts of every creature and gave her secretly to the childless king of Vidarbha, who raised her as Lopamudra. When she grew up, Agastya asked for her hand, and she left the palace for a life of bark garments. When he finally came to her, she spoke up. She would come to him only in the comforts she had grown up with, dressed in jewels on a fine bed, and not in rags. So the great ascetic went to kings to ask for wealth. The journey took him to Ilvala, and at last their son Dridhasyu was born.
variations: In Rig Veda 1.179 she speaks as the aging wife of an ascetic; the Mahabharata supplies the story of her creation and her demand for wealth.
Shri Vidya tradition names one form of the Panchadashi mantra, the Hadi-vidya, the Lopamudra-vidya after her.
Some Tamil and Kodava traditions identify her with the river Kaveri.

bhrigu|brahma|created-by.label: Bhrigu is one of the mind-born sons (Manasaputras) of Brahma (Vishnu Purana 1.7)
bhrigu|brahma|created-by.variation: Vedic texts make him Bhrigu Varuni, son of Varuna; the Mahabharata says he was born from the fire of Varuna's sacrifice

varuna|bhrigu|parent.label: Varuna is the father of Bhrigu Varuni in the Shatapatha Brahmana and Taittiriya Upanishad
varuna|bhrigu|parent.variation: The Puranas make Bhrigu a mind-born son of Brahma

varuna|bhrigu|guru.label: Varuna taught his son Bhrigu to know Brahman through tapas (Taittiriya Upanishad, Bhriguvalli)

svayambhuva-manu|bhrigu|guru.label: Manu taught the law-code to Bhrigu, who recites it to the sages (Manusmriti 1.59–60)

bhrigu|shukracharya|parent.label: Shukra (Ushanas Kavya), guru of the asuras, is a son of Bhrigu (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)
bhrigu|shukracharya|parent.variation: Some Puranas make Shukra the son of Bhrigu's son Kavi, hence the name Kavya

bhrigu|chyavana|parent.label: Chyavana was born to Bhrigu and Puloma; his radiance burned the rakshasa who carried off his mother (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 5–6)

bhrigu|lakshmi|parent.label: Lakshmi was born as Bhargavi, daughter of Bhrigu and Khyati (Vishnu Purana 1.8)
bhrigu|lakshmi|parent.variation: Better known is her rise from the Churning of the Ocean; the Vishnu Purana treats that as her later reappearance

bhrigu|jamadagni|ancestor-of.label: Bhrigu → Chyavana → Aurva → Richika → Jamadagni (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

bhrigu|parashurama|ancestor-of.label: Parashurama, 'Rama of the Bhrigus', is the most famous Bhargava

bhrigu|markandeya|ancestor-of.label: Markandeya, son of Mrikandu, belongs to Bhrigu's lineage (Vishnu Purana 1.10)

bhrigu|vishnu|curse.label: Bhrigu cursed Vishnu to be born again and again among mortals after Vishnu killed Bhrigu's wife for sheltering asuras (Matsya Purana; Devi Bhagavata Purana, Book 4)
bhrigu|vishnu|curse.variation: In the Bhagavata (10.89) Bhrigu kicks Vishnu's chest to test him and then proclaims him supreme, with no curse

bhrigu|agni|curse.label: Bhrigu cursed Agni to devour all things, pure and impure, for betraying Puloma to a rakshasa; Brahma softened the curse (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 5–7)

bhrigu|daksha|ally.label: Bhrigu, Daksha's son-in-law through Khyati, took Daksha's side against Shiva at the sacrifice (Bhagavata Purana 4.2–4.5)

virabhadra|bhrigu|enemy.label: Virabhadra tore out Bhrigu's beard when Shiva's hosts wrecked Daksha's sacrifice (Bhagavata Purana 4.5)

atri|brahma|created-by.label: Atri is a mind-born son of Brahma (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.7)

atri|saptarishi|member-of.label: Atri is in both the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age

atri|anasuya|spouse.label: Atri and Anasuya, the ideal ascetic couple of Chitrakuta

atri|soma|parent.label: Soma, the Moon, is the son of Atri, born from his eyes (Vishnu Purana 4.6; Harivamsha) or from Anasuya (Bhagavata 4.1)
atri|soma|parent.variation: Other accounts have the Moon rise from the Churning of the Ocean; the Rig Veda gives Soma no such parentage

atri|durvasa|parent.label: Durvasa, a portion of Shiva, was born to Atri and Anasuya (Bhagavata Purana 4.1)

atri|dattatreya|parent.label: Dattatreya, 'given to Atri', a portion of Vishnu, was born to Atri and Anasuya (Bhagavata Purana 4.1)

vishnu|atri|boon.label: Pleased by Atri's tapas on Mount Riksha, Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva appeared together and promised to be born as his sons (Bhagavata Purana 4.1)

ashvins|atri|boon.label: The Ashvins rescued Atri from a burning chasm and cooled it for him (Rig Veda 1.116.8, 1.117.3)

atri|surya|ally.label: Atri restored the Sun after the asura Svarbhanu had pierced it with darkness (Rig Veda 5.40)
atri|surya|ally.variation: Later tradition identifies Svarbhanu with Rahu

atri|rama|ally.label: Atri welcomed Rama, Sita and Lakshmana at his hermitage (Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda)

kardama|anasuya|parent.label: Anasuya is a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti (Bhagavata Purana 3.24)

daksha|anasuya|parent.label: The Vishnu Purana (1.7) makes Anasuya a daughter of Daksha and Prasuti
daksha|anasuya|parent.variation: The Bhagavata makes her the daughter of Kardama and Devahuti

anasuya|soma|parent.label: In the Bhagavata (4.1), Soma is Anasuya's son, born of Brahma's portion

anasuya|durvasa|parent.label: Durvasa is the son of Anasuya and Atri (Bhagavata Purana 4.1)

anasuya|dattatreya|parent.label: Dattatreya is the son of Anasuya and Atri (Bhagavata Purana 4.1; Markandeya Purana)

anasuya|sita|boon.label: Anasuya gave Sita a celestial garland, garments, ornaments and an unguent that would never fade (Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda)

marichi|kashyapa|parent.label: Kashyapa is the son of Marichi (Ramayana 1.70; Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65)

kashyapa|aditi|spouse.label: Aditi, daughter of Daksha, is the wife of Kashyapa and mother of the Adityas

kashyapa|diti|spouse.label: Diti, daughter of Daksha, is the wife of Kashyapa and mother of the Daityas

kashyapa|danu|spouse.label: Danu, daughter of Daksha, is the wife of Kashyapa and mother of the Danavas

kashyapa|kadru|spouse.label: Kadru, daughter of Daksha, is the wife of Kashyapa and mother of the Nagas

kashyapa|vinata|spouse.label: Vinata, daughter of Daksha, is the wife of Kashyapa and mother of Aruna and Garuda

kashyapa|adityas|parent.label: The Adityas are the sons of Kashyapa and Aditi (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.15)
kashyapa|adityas|parent.variation: In the Rig Veda the Adityas are sons of Aditi, and no father is named

kashyapa|indra|parent.label: Indra is a son of Kashyapa and Aditi in the epics and Puranas

kashyapa|surya|parent.label: Vivasvan, the Sun, is a son of Kashyapa and Aditi (Ramayana 1.70; Vishnu Purana)

kashyapa|vamana|parent.label: Vishnu was born as Vamana to Kashyapa and Aditi (Bhagavata Purana 8.17–18)

kashyapa|hiranyakashipu|parent.label: Hiranyakashipu was born to Kashyapa and Diti, conceived at the forbidden twilight hour (Bhagavata Purana 3.14)

kashyapa|hiranyaksha|parent.label: Hiranyaksha, Hiranyakashipu's twin, was born to Kashyapa and Diti (Bhagavata Purana 3.14)

kashyapa|garuda|parent.label: Garuda is the son of Kashyapa and Vinata (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

kashyapa|aruna|parent.label: Aruna, charioteer of the Sun, is the son of Kashyapa and Vinata (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

kashyapa|maruts|parent.label: The Maruts came from Diti's embryo by Kashyapa, which Indra split into many parts (Ramayana 1.46; Bhagavata 6.18)
kashyapa|maruts|parent.variation: In the Rig Veda the Maruts are sons of Rudra and Prishni

kashyapa|shesha|parent.label: Shesha is the eldest of the Nagas born to Kashyapa and Kadru (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

kashyapa|vasuki|parent.label: Vasuki is a Naga son of Kashyapa and Kadru (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

kashyapa|takshaka|parent.label: Takshaka is a Naga son of Kashyapa and Kadru (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

kashyapa|saptarishi|member-of.label: Kashyapa is in the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the list for the present Vaivasvata age (Vishnu Purana 3.1)

parashurama|kashyapa|boon.label: After clearing the earth of kshatriyas, Parashurama gave the whole earth to Kashyapa as sacrificial fee (Mahabharata)

angiras|brahma|created-by.label: Angiras is a mind-born son of Brahma (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.7)
angiras|brahma|created-by.variation: In the Rig Veda the Angirases are a clan of ancestral priests

angiras|saptarishi|member-of.label: Angiras is in the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age (Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vashistha)

angiras|brihaspati|parent.label: Brihaspati, priest of the gods, is a son of Angiras (Angirasa)

angiras|indra|ally.label: The Angirases sang open the Vala cave with Indra and freed the cows and the light (Rig Veda 1.62; 10.108)

angiras|vala|enemy.label: The Angirases' chant helped split the rock-cave Vala (Rig Veda 1.62, 4.1)

angiras|agni|ally.label: Agni is called the first of the Angirases (Rig Veda 1.1.6, 1.31.1); the Mahabharata tells how Angiras once took over Agni's role

angiras|bharadvaja|ancestor-of.label: Bharadvaja, son of Brihaspati, is a grandson of Angiras

angiras|gautama|ancestor-of.label: The Gautamas are a branch of the Angirasa clan in the gotra lists

angiras|kacha|ancestor-of.label: Kacha, son of Brihaspati, is a grandson of Angiras

pulastya|brahma|created-by.label: Pulastya is a mind-born son of Brahma (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.7)

pulastya|saptarishi|member-of.label: Pulastya is in the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age

pulastya|vishrava|parent.label: Vishrava was born to Pulastya and Trinabindu's daughter (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 2)

pulastya|ravana|ancestor-of.label: Ravana is Pulastya's grandson through Vishrava, hence the name Paulastya

pulastya|kubera|ancestor-of.label: Kubera is Pulastya's grandson through Vishrava (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 3)

pulastya|kumbhakarna|ancestor-of.label: Kumbhakarna is Pulastya's grandson through Vishrava

pulastya|vibhishana|ancestor-of.label: Vibhishana is Pulastya's grandson through Vishrava

pulastya|parashara|boon.label: Because Parashara gave up his sacrifice to destroy the rakshasas, Pulastya blessed him to compose a Purana (Vishnu Purana 1.1)

pulastya|kartavirya-arjuna|ally.label: Pulastya persuaded Kartavirya Arjuna to release his captive grandson Ravana (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 33)

pulastya|bhishma|guru.label: Pulastya taught Bhishma the merits of pilgrimage to the tirthas (Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirthayatra section)

pulastya|agastya|parent.label: The Bhagavata (4.1) names Agastya a son of Pulastya and Havirbhu
pulastya|agastya|parent.variation: The Rig Veda and the epics say Agastya was born of Mitra and Varuna in a jar

pulastya|pulaha|sibling.label: Pulastya and Pulaha are brothers among Brahma's mind-born sons and are usually named together

pulaha|brahma|created-by.label: Pulaha is a mind-born son of Brahma, born from his navel in the Bhagavata (3.12)

pulaha|saptarishi|member-of.label: Pulaha is in the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age

pulaha|kardama|parent.label: The Vishnu Purana (1.10) makes Kardama a son of Pulaha and Kshama
pulaha|kardama|parent.variation: The Bhagavata says Kardama was born from Brahma's shadow and makes Pulaha his son-in-law through Gati

pulaha|kratu|sibling.label: Pulaha and Kratu are brothers among Brahma's mind-born sons

kratu|brahma|created-by.label: Kratu is a mind-born son of Brahma (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.7)

kratu|saptarishi|member-of.label: Kratu is in the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age

kratu|marichi|sibling.label: Kratu and Marichi are brothers among Brahma's mind-born sons

marichi|brahma|created-by.label: Marichi is usually named first among Brahma's mind-born sons (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 65; Vishnu Purana 1.7)

marichi|saptarishi|member-of.label: Marichi heads the Puranic list for the Svayambhuva age

marichi|vaivasvata-manu|ancestor-of.label: Brahma → Marichi → Kashyapa → Vivasvan → Manu, at the head of the Ikshvaku genealogy (Ramayana 1.70)

marichi|maruts|member-of.label: The Bhagavad Gita (10.21) names Marichi as chief of the Maruts
marichi|maruts|member-of.variation: Many commentators take this Marichi to be a different figure from the Prajapati

vashistha|brahma|created-by.label: Vashistha is a mind-born son of Brahma in the Puranas (Vishnu Purana 1.7)
vashistha|brahma|created-by.variation: The Rig Veda has him born of Mitra and Varuna; the Puranas reconcile the two by a second birth after Nimi's curse

mitra|vashistha|parent.label: Vashistha was born of Mitra and Varuna, from the mind of Urvashi (Rig Veda 7.33.11)

varuna|vashistha|parent.label: Vashistha is Maitravaruni, son of Mitra and Varuna (Rig Veda 7.33.11)

vashistha|saptarishi|member-of.label: Vashistha is in both the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the Puranic lists

vashistha|arundhati|spouse.label: Vashistha and Arundhati, the model couple, are shown to brides as the stars Mizar and Alcor

vashistha|shakti-rishi|parent.label: Shakti (Shaktri) is the eldest of Vashistha's hundred sons (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

vashistha|parashara|ancestor-of.label: Parashara is Vashistha's grandson through Shakti, raised by Vashistha after Shakti's death

vashistha|vyasa|ancestor-of.label: Vyasa is Vashistha's great-grandson: Vashistha → Shakti → Parashara → Vyasa

vashistha|vishvamitra|enemy.label: The feud between Vashistha and Vishvamitra over the wish-fulfilling cow, and over brahmin against kshatriya power (Ramayana 1.51–56; Mahabharata, Adi Parva)
vashistha|vishvamitra|enemy.variation: The Rig Veda shows both sages as rival priests of King Sudas (Mandalas 3 and 7)

vashistha|rama|guru.label: Vashistha is Rama's family guru and teacher (Ramayana; framed as his teacher in the Yoga Vasishtha)

vashistha|bharata|guru.label: Vashistha guided Bharata after Dasharatha's death and during Rama's exile (Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda)

vashistha|dasharatha|guru.label: Vashistha is Dasharatha's purohita (royal priest) and adviser

vashistha|ikshvaku|guru.label: Vashistha has been purohita of the Ikshvaku line since its founder (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda)

vashistha|nandini|ally.label: Nandini is Vashistha's wish-fulfilling cow, whom Vishvamitra tried to seize (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)
vashistha|nandini|ally.variation: In the Ramayana the cow is called Shabala

vashistha|vasus|curse.label: Vashistha cursed the eight Vasus to be born as mortals for stealing Nandini; Dyu was reborn as Bhishma (Mahabharata, Adi Parva 93)

vashistha|trishanku|curse.label: Vashistha branded Satyavrata with three sins (tri-shanku), which gave him his name (Harivamsha 1.13)
vashistha|trishanku|curse.variation: In the Ramayana (1.58) it is Vashistha's sons who curse Trishanku to become an outcaste

vashistha|agastya|sibling.label: Both were born from the seed of Mitra and Varuna in a jar at the sight of Urvashi (Rig Veda 7.33.13)

kardama|arundhati|parent.label: Arundhati is a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti (Bhagavata Purana 3.24)
kardama|arundhati|parent.variation: The Vishnu Purana names Vashistha's wife Urja, a daughter of Daksha

arundhati|shakti-rishi|parent.label: Arundhati is the mother of Shakti, eldest son of Vashistha

arundhati|brahma|created-by.label: The Shiva Purana says Arundhati was once Sandhya, a mind-born daughter of Brahma, reborn as the daughter of Medhatithi

shiva|arundhati|boon.label: Pleased by Arundhati's tapas during a twelve-year drought, Shiva blessed her and made the place a tirtha, Badarapachana (Mahabharata, Shalya Parva)

vishvamitra|saptarishi|member-of.label: Vishvamitra is in the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the list for the present Vaivasvata age

vishvamitra|rama|guru.label: Vishvamitra taught Rama the Bala and Atibala mantras and gave him divine astras (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)

vishvamitra|lakshmana|guru.label: Vishvamitra took Lakshmana, with Rama, to guard his sacrifice and taught them both (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)

vishvamitra|trishanku|ally.label: Vishvamitra sent Trishanku to heaven in his own body and made a new heaven of stars when Indra pushed him back (Ramayana 1.57–60)

vishvamitra|shunahshepa|guru.label: Vishvamitra taught Shunahshepa the hymns that freed him from being sacrificed (Ramayana 1.61–62)
vishvamitra|shunahshepa|guru.variation: In the Aitareya Brahmana (7.13–18) Vishvamitra adopts him as his eldest son, Devarata

vishvamitra|shakuntala|parent.label: Shakuntala is the daughter of Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

brahma|vishvamitra|boon.label: After his long tapas, Brahma recognised Vishvamitra as a brahmarshi (Ramayana 1.65)

vishvamitra|rambha|curse.label: Vishvamitra cursed Rambha, sent by Indra to seduce him, to become a rock for ten thousand years (Ramayana 1.64)

vishvamitra|harishchandra|enemy.label: Vishvamitra stripped Harishchandra of kingdom, family and freedom to test his truthfulness (Markandeya Purana 7–8)
vishvamitra|harishchandra|enemy.variation: The ordeal is a test and ends in Harishchandra's vindication; the Aitareya Brahmana's version does not include it

vishvamitra|maricha|enemy.label: Maricha disrupted Vishvamitra's sacrifice until Rama drove him away (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)

vishvamitra|subahu|enemy.label: Subahu disrupted Vishvamitra's sacrifice and was killed by Rama (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)

vishvamitra|shakti-rishi|enemy.label: Vishvamitra sent a rakshasa into King Kalmashapada, who then devoured Vashistha's son Shakti (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

jamadagni|saptarishi|member-of.label: Jamadagni is in the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the list for the present Vaivasvata age

jamadagni|renuka|spouse.label: Renuka, a princess, is the wife of Jamadagni

jamadagni|parashurama|parent.label: Parashurama is the youngest son of Jamadagni and Renuka

kartavirya-arjuna|jamadagni|enemy.label: Kartavirya Arjuna carried off the calf of Jamadagni's sacrificial cow, which led to Parashurama's revenge (Mahabharata, Vana Parva 116)

gautama|saptarishi|member-of.label: Gotama is in the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the list for the present Vaivasvata age

gautama|ahalya|spouse.label: Ahalya is the wife of Gautama (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)

gautama|indra|curse.label: Gautama cursed Indra to lose his testicles for seducing Ahalya (Ramayana 1.48)

gautama|kripa|ancestor-of.label: Kripa, born to Sharadvan son of Gautama, bears the name Gautama (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

ahalya|brahma|created-by.label: Brahma fashioned Ahalya as the most flawless of women and gave her to Gautama (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 30)
ahalya|brahma|created-by.variation: The Mahabharata and Harivamsha make her a daughter of the Puru king Mudgala

indra|ahalya|enemy.label: Indra seduced Ahalya disguised as Gautama (Shatapatha Brahmana 3.3.4.18; Ramayana 1.48)
indra|ahalya|enemy.variation: No edge type fits exactly. In Valmiki's Bala Kanda Ahalya knowingly consents; in the Uttara Kanda and later texts she is deceived

rama|ahalya|boon.label: Rama's arrival at Gautama's hermitage ended Ahalya's curse (Ramayana 1.49)
rama|ahalya|boon.variation: In the Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas, the touch of Rama's foot brings her back from stone

ahalya|anjana|parent.label: In some regional and Southeast Asian Ramayanas (e.g. the Thai Ramakien), Anjana is a daughter of Gautama and Ahalya

bharadvaja|saptarishi|member-of.label: Bharadvaja is in the Vedic list (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.2.6) and the list for the present Vaivasvata age

brihaspati|bharadvaja|parent.label: Bharadvaja Barhaspatya is a son of Brihaspati, by Mamata in the Puranas (Bhagavata 9.20; Vishnu Purana 4.19)

bharadvaja|drona|parent.label: Drona was born in a vessel (drona) from Bharadvaja's seed, shed at the sight of the apsara Ghritachi (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

indra|bharadvaja|guru.label: Indra taught Bharadvaja the endlessness of the Veda (Taittiriya Brahmana 3.10.11) and the science of Ayurveda (Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 1)

bharadvaja|rama|ally.label: Bharadvaja hosted Rama at Prayaga and directed him to Chitrakuta (Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 54)

bharadvaja|bharata|ally.label: Bharadvaja feasted Bharata's whole army through his ascetic power (Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 91)

bharadvaja|kubera|ancestor-of.label: Bharadvaja is Kubera's maternal grandfather: his daughter Devavarnini (Ilavida) married Vishrava (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 3)

valmiki|bharadvaja|guru.label: A disciple named Bharadvaja goes with Valmiki at the opening of the Ramayana (1.2)
valmiki|bharadvaja|guru.variation: It is unclear whether this disciple is the Vedic seer

bharadvaja|bharata-king|ally.label: The Maruts gave the abandoned infant Bharadvaja to King Bharata, who adopted him (Vishnu Purana 4.19; Bhagavata 9.20)

dadhichi|ashvins|guru.label: Dadhyanch taught the Ashvins the secret Madhu-vidya through a horse's head (Rig Veda 1.116.12, 1.117.22; Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.16–17)

ashvins|dadhichi|boon.label: The Ashvins gave Dadhyanch a horse's head so that he could teach them without breaking Indra's threat (Shatapatha Brahmana 14.1.1)

dadhichi|indra|ally.label: Dadhichi gave up his life so that his bones could become Indra's vajra (Rig Veda 1.84.13; Mahabharata, Vana Parva 100; Bhagavata 6.10)

dadhichi|shiva|devotee.label: Shaiva Puranas praise Dadhichi as a great devotee of Shiva (Shiva Purana; Linga Purana)

dadhichi|daksha|enemy.label: Dadhichi rebuked Daksha for leaving Shiva out of the sacrifice and walked out (Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita)

dadhichi|vishnu|enemy.label: The Linga Purana tells of Dadhichi defeating Vishnu in a dispute over King Kshuva
dadhichi|vishnu|enemy.variation: This is a Shaiva sectarian episode not found in Vaishnava texts

chyavana|sukanya|spouse.label: King Sharyati gave his daughter Sukanya to Chyavana after she blinded him by mistake (Shatapatha Brahmana 4.1.5)

ashvins|chyavana|boon.label: The Ashvins made the aged Chyavana young again (Rig Veda 1.116.10; Shatapatha Brahmana 4.1.5)

chyavana|ashvins|boon.label: Chyavana won the Ashvins a share of soma at Sharyati's sacrifice (Mahabharata, Vana Parva 124)

chyavana|indra|enemy.label: When Indra raised the vajra against him, Chyavana froze his arm and conjured the demon Mada (Mahabharata, Vana Parva 124)

chyavana|jamadagni|ancestor-of.label: Chyavana → Aurva → Richika → Jamadagni (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)

chyavana|vishvamitra|boon.label: Pleased by King Kushika's patience, Chyavana foretold that Kushika's grandson Vishvamitra would become a brahmin (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva)

nahusha|chyavana|ally.label: King Nahusha ransomed Chyavana from fishermen, valuing him as highly as a cow (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva)

chyavana|dadhichi|parent.label: Some Puranas make Dadhicha a son of Chyavana and Sukanya
chyavana|dadhichi|parent.variation: The Rig Veda calls Dadhyanch a son of Atharvan

vaivasvata-manu|sukanya|ancestor-of.label: Sukanya is the daughter of Sharyati, son of Manu (Shatapatha Brahmana 4.1.5; Bhagavata 9.3)

ashvins|sukanya|ally.label: The Ashvins tried to win Sukanya; she stayed faithful and in return told them how to gain their place at the sacrifice (Shatapatha Brahmana 4.1.5)

sukanya|jamadagni|ancestor-of.label: In Puranic genealogies Jamadagni descends from Chyavana and Sukanya through Apnavana, Aurva and Richika
sukanya|jamadagni|ancestor-of.variation: The Mahabharata names Arushi, not Sukanya, as Aurva's mother

mitra|agastya|parent.label: Agastya was born from the seed of Mitra and Varuna in a jar, hence Kumbhayoni (Rig Veda 7.33.13)

varuna|agastya|parent.label: Agastya is Maitravaruni, son of Mitra and Varuna (Rig Veda 7.33.13)

agastya|lopamudra|spouse.label: Agastya and Lopamudra, who speak together in Rig Veda 1.179

lopamudra|agastya|created-by.label: Agastya created Lopamudra from the finest features of all creatures and gave her to the king of Vidarbha to raise (Mahabharata, Vana Parva 94)

agastya|vatapi|slayer.label: Agastya ate and digested Vatapi, who had been served to him as meat (Mahabharata, Vana Parva 97; Ramayana 3.11)

agastya|ilvala|slayer.label: Agastya burned Ilvala to ashes with his gaze (Ramayana 3.11)
agastya|ilvala|slayer.variation: In the Mahabharata Ilvala is subdued and gives Agastya wealth

agastya|rama|guru.label: Agastya gave Rama Vishnu's bow, inexhaustible quivers and a sword (Ramayana 3.12) and taught him the Aditya Hridaya
agastya|rama|guru.variation: The Aditya Hridaya is in the vulgate Yuddha Kanda but not in the Critical Edition

agastya|nahusha|curse.label: Agastya cursed the arrogant Nahusha, who had become Indra, to fall to earth as a serpent (Mahabharata, Udyoga and Anushasana Parvas)
agastya|nahusha|curse.variation: In the Anushasana Parva, Bhrigu, hidden in Agastya's matted hair, speaks the curse

agastya|tataka|curse.label: Agastya cursed Tataka to become a man-eating rakshasi (Ramayana 1.25)

agastya|maricha|curse.label: Agastya cursed Maricha, Tataka's son, to become a rakshasa (Ramayana 1.25)

agastya|indra|ally.label: Agastya drank the ocean dry so that Indra and the gods could destroy the Kalakeya asuras hiding in it (Mahabharata, Vana Parva)

hayagriva|agastya|guru.label: Hayagriva taught Agastya the glory of Lalita and her thousand names (Brahmanda Purana, Lalitopakhyana)

kartikeya|agastya|guru.label: Tamil tradition says Murugan (Kartikeya) taught Agastya the Tamil language

agastya|tripura-sundari|devotee.label: Agastya receives and spreads the worship of Lalita Tripura Sundari (Brahmanda Purana, Lalitopakhyana)

lopamudra|tripura-sundari|devotee.label: Shri Vidya tradition names one form of the goddess's mantra, the Hadi-vidya, after Lopamudra as a leading devotee
lopamudra|tripura-sundari|devotee.variation: This comes from later Tantric tradition, not the Vedas or epics
